questions.question: In a bus scheduling model, the day is split into six four-hour intervals and every bus operates for two consecutive intervals. What does the decision variable $x_i$ count?
options: Buses that are on the road during interval $i$
Buses that end their shift in interval $i$
Buses required to be on the road in interval $i$
Buses that start their shift in interval $i$

questions.question: In a cyclic bus scheduling model, $x_i$ buses start in interval $i$, each runs two consecutive intervals, and interval $i$ has requirement $d_i$. Why is coverage written as $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ rather than $x_{i-1}+x_i=d_i$?
options: Buses beyond $d_i$ are wasted, so $\ge$ is just a softer $=$
With $\ge$, the busiest interval no longer has to be met
The requirement $d_i$ is an upper limit on the buses used
More than $d_i$ buses may be on the road in interval $i$

questions.question: A cyclic bus model covers the midnight–4 AM interval by $x_6+x_1\ge4$, where $x_6$ buses start at 8 PM and $x_1$ at midnight, and each bus runs eight hours. Which assumption justifies the $x_6$ term?
options: The schedule repeats daily, so 8 PM starters run past midnight
No bus is on the road before midnight, so $x_6$ is set to zero
Buses starting at 8 PM are counted twice to cover the night
The midnight interval is merged with the 8 PM interval

questions.question: In the cyclic bus model, the day has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, 2: 4–8 AM, 3: 8 AM–noon, 4: noon–4 PM, 5: 4–8 PM, 6: 8 PM–midnight); $x_i$ buses start in interval $i$ and each runs two consecutive intervals; requirements are $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. Which constraint covers 8 AM–noon?

The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. Which coverage constraints does $x=(1,7,3,4,8,3)$ violate?
options: Only the midnight–4 AM interval
Only the 8 PM–midnight interval
Both midnight–4 AM and 8 PM–midnight
None; all six intervals are covered

questions.question: In a bus model, $x_i$ buses start in four-hour interval $i$ and run two intervals; noon–4 PM needs $x_3+x_4\ge7$ and 4–8 PM needs $x_4+x_5\ge12$. With $x_3=2$ and $x_5=9$ fixed, what is the smallest $x_4$ meeting both?

In a cyclic bus model, $x_i$ buses start in interval $i$ ($i=1,\dots,6$) and each runs two consecutive intervals; requirements $d_i$ give $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. If each bus starting in interval $i$ costs $c_i$ per day, which objective minimizes total daily cost?
options: $\min\sum_{i=1}^6c_ix_i$
$\min\sum_{i=1}^6c_id_i$
$\min\sum_{i=1}^6x_i$

questions.question: For six four-hour intervals with requirements $d_i$, a student defines $y_i$ as the buses on the road in interval $i$ and minimizes $\sum_{i}y_i$ subject to $y_i\ge d_i$, where every bus runs two consecutive intervals. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: setting $y_i=d_i$ gives the fewest buses possible
Only the integer restriction on the $y_i$ is missing
It counts each bus twice and loses the two-interval link
Only the wrap-around from 8 PM to midnight is missing

questions.question: The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. Its minimum is 26 buses. If one requirement $d_i$ is raised by 1, what happens to the minimum?
options: It rises by exactly 1, since one more bus is needed
It rises by at least 1, since the old plan fails
It rises by up to 2, since a bus covers two intervals
It rises by at most 1, and it need not rise at all

questions.question: The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. With $x_1=0$, $x_2=8$, $x_3=2$ fixed, what is the smallest possible value of $x_4+x_5+x_6$?

A cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, 2: 4–8 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$ and 4–8 AM requirement 8. If each bus ran 12 hours (three consecutive intervals), which constraint would cover 4–8 AM?

The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. Ignoring integrality, a solver returns $x=(0.5,7.5,2.5,4.5,7.5,3.5)$ with 26 buses. What can be said of rounding every $x_i$ up?
options: It is infeasible, as it under-covers 4–8 AM
It is feasible and optimal, still using 26 buses
It is feasible with 29 buses, 3 more than needed
It is feasible with 32 buses, 6 more than needed

questions.question: The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. Why would replacing every $\ge$ by $=$ leave no schedule at all?
options: Six equations in six unknowns never have a nonnegative solution
Equations 1, 3, 5 give $\sum x_i=26$; 2, 4, 6 give $\sum x_i=19$
Exact coverage would force some $x_i$ to be fractional, not whole
The wrap-around equation $x_6+x_1=4$ would force $x_6=x_1=2$

questions.question: The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. A planner replaces $x_6+x_1\ge4$ by $x_1\ge4$. The cyclic minimum is 26; $x=(4,4,6,1,11,0)$ uses 26 buses. Which statement is correct?
options: Planner-feasible plans are cyclic-feasible; 26 is still reachable
Cyclic-feasible plans are planner-feasible, so 26 is still reachable
Planner-feasible plans are fewer, so the minimum must exceed 26
The planner's constraint has one term fewer, so the minimum drops

questions.question: The cyclic bus model has six four-hour intervals (1: midnight–4 AM, …, 6: 8 PM–midnight), $x_i$ buses starting in interval $i$, each running two consecutive intervals, requirements $d=(4,8,10,7,12,4)$ and constraints $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ with $x_0=x_6$. The schedule $x=(0,8,2,5,7,4)$ is feasible with 26 buses. Which argument proves that no feasible schedule uses fewer?
options: Intervals 2, 4, 6 give $\sum x_i\ge8+7+4=19$
All six intervals give $2\sum x_i\ge4+8+\dots+4=45$
Interval 5 alone gives $\sum x_i\ge x_4+x_5\ge12$
Intervals 1, 3, 5 give $\sum x_i\ge4+10+12=26$

questions.question: In the bus model $\min\sum_i x_i$ subject to $x_{i-1}+x_i\ge d_i$ ($x_0=x_6$) and $x_i\ge0$, all requirements $d_i$ are integers. Why must each $x_i$ still be required to be an integer?
options: Integer $d_i$ do not prevent a fractional continuous optimum
Integer restrictions lower the minimum number of buses
Without them, the coverage constraints are not linear
Without them, the continuous model has no optimum

questions.question: A cyclic bus model lets $x_i$ buses start an eight-hour shift in four-hour interval $i$, with requirements $d_i$, and minimizes $\sum_{i=1}^6x_i$ as the number of buses needed. Which assumption makes this sum equal the number of buses?
options: No bus starts a second shift on the same day
The day repeats, so the model sets $x_0=x_6$
Each interval is covered by exactly $d_i$ buses
Every $x_i$ has the same objective coefficient
